II. Proving That God Knows Himself

After recalling the points we have already established, you may feel that no further proof is needed to show that God knows Himself. Still, let us make the point clearer. The reality of knowledge is the reality of existence, provided it is free of deficiencies and the veils of darkness. We have shown that whatever exists independently and is free of what accompanies it is present to itself. So it is understood by itself, and its knowing itself is nothing other than its own existence. This presence does not require a difference between what is present and what it is present to, either in reality or in the mind.

The stronger a thing's existence, the more fully it is present and the more free it is of deficiency and limitation. It is therefore more fully intellect, more fully intelligible, and more fully knowing itself. Since the Necessary Being is the source of all levels of existence—the intellectual and sensory, the created and the coming-to-be—He is at the highest level of strength and immateriality. His existence is unlimited in its intensity. Other things, even if they were unlimited in number or duration, would still not reach a level of intensity beyond which no further level could exist. The Necessary Being is infinitely beyond even an infinite degree of existence. His self-knowledge is therefore to other separate beings' self-knowledge as His existence is to theirs. The true existent knows Himself with the fullest knowledge, radiant and manifest beyond comparison. Just as the existence of possible things is gathered up and surpassed in His existence, as we have proved, so their knowledge is gathered up and surpassed in His knowledge of Himself.

We have also shown that God's existence is the reality of existence, from which no existent is excluded. In the same way, His knowledge of Himself is the reality of knowledge, from which no knowledge or known thing is absent. Recall what you have learned in first philosophy and general philosophy: whenever reason judges that something is a perfection for a being simply insofar as it exists, and that it entails no restriction to a lower kind, no change, no body, and no composition, if this perfection is found in any existent, then it can also belong to the true existent. It must belong to Him; otherwise, He would have a possibility opposed to His necessary existence. We have already shown that the Necessary Being is necessary in every respect. Knowledge is plainly a perfection of anything that exists, and it entails no body, change, or limited possibility. Since many existents, such as intellects, possess it, it must belong to God by necessity.

How could anyone with sound judgment accept that the giver and source of a perfection lacks that perfection, making the receiver nobler than the giver and the one who benefits more honored than the one who gives? We have established that all possible things depend on God, whose essence is pure necessity and pure actuality. Among the things that depend on Him are knowing beings and cognitive forms. The giver of all things possesses every perfection fully, without being made multiple by them. Otherwise, He would lack the very perfection He gives. So the Necessary Being knows, and His knowledge is not something added to His essence, as we have shown.
III. God's Knowledge of Everything Other Than Himself

In general discussions of knowledge, we established that complete knowledge of a complete cause—or of the aspect that makes it a cause—entails complete knowledge of its effect. Do not understand “the causal aspect” to mean the relation of causality itself, which comes into being only after both cause and effect. It means what comes before the effect and makes the cause its cause, the reality through which the effect comes to exist.

Every effect depends for its existence on something that gives it its own definite reality, without depending on anything else. Otherwise, it and that other thing together would be what gives rise to the effect. Here we are discussing what independently gives the effect its existence. So an independent cause must have its effect as one of its necessary consequences. Every effect follows from the specific cause that brings it about. Whenever that cause exists in its full identity, whether in thought or outside it, the particular effect follows, because it belongs to the cause's own reality.

The reverse is not true. An effect does not require its specific cause, for then the cause would itself be caused by its own effect. The effect only requires some cause, because it is possible and dependent. So whenever a specific cause is present, the particular effect is present; whenever an effect is present, some cause must be present, but not necessarily the specific cause. The existence of a cause proves with certainty that its particular effect exists. The existence of an effect proves with certainty that there is some cause, but only suggests which particular cause it has. That is why reasoning from an effect to a cause counts as a kind of demonstration only in one sense of the word. Thus, knowing the complete cause, or the aspect by which it brings about its effect, leads to knowledge of the effect. Indeed, a thing with a cause can be known only through knowing its cause.

With this general principle established, we can say: God knows Himself, and His essence is the cause of everything else in an ordered sequence. He directly gives rise to the first being; through it, to the second; through both, to the third; and so on, to every existent. He must therefore know all things in the most perfect order. His knowledge of everything other than Himself follows from His knowledge of Himself, just as the existence of all else follows from His existence.

But how does He know things in a way that does not make His essence or real attributes multiple, or make Him both an agent and a receiver? Nor should His knowledge of things make Him compelled to act because of that knowledge. Does He know things before they exist, after they exist, or along with them—so that He knows them only when they exist? If created things affect His knowledge, or bring about a state in Him that was not there before, then He would not be necessary in every respect. To find the right answer is among the highest forms of human perfection. Whoever attains this understanding becomes like the holy beings, even one of the company of the angels nearest to God. Because the question is difficult and subtle, many learned people have gone astray. Avicenna and his followers said that God's knowledge is something added to His essence. The leading Stoic philosopher and his followers denied that God knows things before bringing them into existence. If these two men, with all their intelligence, skill, and long study of this subject, fell into error, how much more likely are those who follow their own desires and innovations, or argue only to win disputes.

Because of this difficulty, some ancient philosophers denied that God knows any existent other than Himself and the attributes that are His essence. Some went further and denied that He knows anything at all. They thought knowledge was a relation between the knower and the known, and that there could be no such relation between a thing and itself. Or they thought knowledge was an image added to the known thing and equal to it, which would imply more than one Necessary Being. They reasoned that if God did not know Himself, He could not know anything else, because knowing something else depends on first knowing oneself. They went far astray and suffered a clear loss.

How ugly and wrong it is for a created being to claim that it can know the great realities of the heavenly realm and the subtle details of the spiritual world, call itself a philosopher and wise person, and then deny its wise and knowing Creator any knowledge of anything at all—the Creator who gave existence to those who know and lit their hearts with knowledge. Perhaps those ancient philosophers meant something other than their words seem to say, or perhaps they used “knowledge” in a special sense. They may have meant to deny God the kind of receptive knowledge humans have, or mental images divided into concepts and judgments, or something like these. God knows best the hidden intentions of His servants.
IV. A Survey of Views on God's Knowledge of Things

There are several well-known views on how God knows things. The first is held by followers of Aristotle's school, including al-Fārābī, Avicenna, Bahmanyār, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Lawkarī, and many later thinkers. They say that the forms of possible things are present in God's essence as mental forms, as general forms. The second view is that the actual existence of things—whether they are immaterial or material, simple or composite—is what makes God know them. This was the view of Shihāb al-Dīn Suhrawardī, the leading figure among the Illuminationists, and of those who followed him, including Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi, Ibn Kammūna, al-Shīrāzī, and Muḥammad al-Shahrazūrī, author of The Divine Tree.

The third view says that God is united with the intelligible forms. This view is attributed to Porphyry, one of the greatest students of Aristotle and a leading figure in Aristotle's school. The fourth is Plato's view: separate Forms, or intelligible Ideas, are divine knowledge through which God knows all beings. The fifth view belongs to the Muʿtazilites, who say that possible things exist as “things” before they exist in reality, and that God knows them eternally through this prior existence. A related view is attributed to the Sufis: things are established in God's knowledge before they exist in the world.

The sixth view says that God's essence is one general knowledge of all possible things. Most later thinkers hold this view. They say God has two kinds of knowledge of things: a general knowledge that comes before them, and a detailed knowledge that accompanies them. The seventh view says that God knows the First Effect in detail and everything else in a general way. The First Effect, in turn, knows the second effect in detail and everything else generally, and so on down the chain of beings.

These are the views most often discussed. One can also lay out the possibilities in a more systematic way. Anyone who says that God knows existing things must decide whether this knowledge is separate from His essence. If it is separate, then either nonexistent things are already established—outside the mind, as the Muʿtazilites say, or in the mind, as some Sufi masters say—or they are not. In the latter case, the separate knowledge may consist of Forms that exist in themselves, apart from God and the things known. These are Plato's Forms. Or God's knowledge of things may be the things themselves: they are knowledge insofar as they are present to God and exist through Him, and known things insofar as they exist in themselves, with their changing matter, their succession, and their differences of time and place. On this view, God's knowledge does not change; the things known do.

If knowledge is not separate from God's essence, it may still be something other than His essence, as al-Fārābī and Avicenna say; or it may be identical with His essence. In the latter case, God may be united with the intelligible forms, as Porphyry and some followers of Aristotle say, or His essence may be one general knowledge of everything other than Himself, or of everything except the First Effect. These are eight possible views. We will examine their strengths and weaknesses, correct what can be corrected, and then identify the view closest to the truth—the truth that comes from God, the Mighty and Generous.
V. Examining the Muʿtazilite View and a View Attributed to the Sufis

The Muʿtazilites say that a nonexistent thing is still a thing: before it exists, it is already distinct from other nonexistent things, and God knows future events eternally through this prior status. To clear thinking, this is a weak and mistaken view. The books of theology and philosophy have already shown why something nonexistent cannot be a thing.

The Sufi masters have been reported to say something similar. Taken at face value, their words have the same flaw: something cannot be established apart from existence, whether in the world or in the mind, whether it is never created or will exist later. To distinguish these cases in that way is arbitrary. Still, we think well of these great teachers. Their books contain subtle insights, profound discoveries, and difficult truths that agree with what God has opened to our hearts—truths about which we have no doubt, as surely as we do not doubt that the sun shines at midday. So we will give their words a sound and noble interpretation. Their apparent meaning is not, on close examination, any less implausible than the Muʿtazilite view.

Among the passages at issue is one in the Meccan Revelations. Ibn Arabi says that, while possible things are nonexistent, they see and are seen, hear and are heard—not with ordinary sight or hearing, but through an abiding kind of seeing and hearing. God chooses whichever of these things He wills and addresses it with His command, expressed in Arabic as “Be.” The thing hears the command and hastens to obey. It comes to be through God's word—or, in a sense, it is that very word. Even in their timeless nonexistence, possible things know the Necessary Being, praise Him, and glorify Him with an eternal praise, though none of them has an existing individual form.

In The Bezels of Wisdom, Ibn Arabi says that knowledge follows what is known. A person who is faithful in the way his own reality is fixed while he is nonexistent will appear in that form when he exists. God knows beforehand how he will be. That is why God says that He knows best who is guided. God also says, “My word does not change,” because His word about creation accords with His knowledge of it. God does not make people unbelievers and then demand what they cannot do. He brings them forth according to what He knows of them, and He knows them as they have made themselves to be. If this is injustice, then they have wronged themselves. God says, “We did not wrong them; they wronged themselves.” God only says to them what His own reality gives Him to say; He knows Himself as He is, including what He will say and what He will not say. He speaks only as He knows He will speak. The command comes from Him; whether they obey or refuse is theirs.

Elsewhere Ibn Arabi says that God gives existence to things according to what their fixed realities call for. Read in their ordinary sense, these words suggest that essences exist in themselves before existence. In that respect, the Sufi view would be no different from the Muʿtazilite view. But reason shows that an essence cannot precede existence, not even in its own nature, much less as something independently real. It makes no difference whether this prior status is called “known existence” or “external existence.”

We must, however, distinguish two ways in which many things may be present. They may all be present through one simple existence, or each may have its own distinct existence, matching its specific nature. When we say that a horse exists in the world or in the mind, we usually mean the horse's own distinct existence—the existence that makes it an actual horse, different from a human being, an elephant, or a cow. A single, simple existence may contain the realities of many kinds in a higher, unified way, though those kinds differ in meaning. Such existence is not ordinarily called the existence of any one of those kinds.

On this distinction, what reason rules out is an essence wholly cut off from existence, whether the existence in question is distinct or simple. But there is no contradiction in saying that an essence is fixed before its own particular existence—the existence that makes it a definite thing, distinct from others. Careful inquiry and sound insight, as we will explain, require this distinction. So when the knowers say that fixed entities, while nonexistent, call for a certain outcome or have a certain character, they mean that these entities lack their own separate existence in the world. They do not mean that they lack all existence. God's existence encompasses them all, since they are implications of His names. His many names and attributes, beyond counting, exist through one simple existence. The fixed entities were never absolutely nonexistent before their particular forms appeared; what they lack from eternity is only that later, limited kind of existence. This is the deep difference between the Sufi way and the Muʿtazilite way.

We have already offered a glimpse of this in discussing the divisions of God's names and attributes. The world of the names is vast. You will see that this approach comes close to an ancient view: before things exist, God's knowledge of them is a simple, eternal intellect. In its simplicity, eternity, and necessary existence, that intellect is all things in a higher, nobler, and purer way. Just as things have a natural existence in this world, an imaginal and particular existence in another world, and a universal intellectual existence above both, they also have a divine, name-based existence in the realm of lordship. The Sufis call this the World of the Names.
VI. Plato’s Forms Apart from Matter, and the View Attributed to Porphyry

We have defended the Platonists' view of separate Ideas. We argued for it and strengthened its case in the discussion of universal knowledge in the First Journey. But whether these Ideas are what make up God's eternal and perfect knowledge, prior to everything else, is another matter. God's knowledge is eternal and necessary through Himself, while these Ideas exist after Him and after His knowledge of them. How, then, can they themselves be His knowledge of things from all eternity?

The same problem arises if these separate Ideas are real beings rather than mental forms: how does God know them before they proceed from Him? Either that leads to an endless chain of forms, or it means God does not know many things until they exist and learns of them from those things. Both possibilities conflict with the principles we have established.

As for the view attributed to Porphyry, Avicenna and many later philosophers have ridiculed and rejected it, as one can see in Avicenna's Healing, Salvation, and Pointers, in Suhrawardī's works, in Bahmanyār's The Book of Attainment, in al-Tusi, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, and others. We have already discussed this question at length in the section on the unity of the intellect and the intelligible. Anyone who wants to understand the view and see its depth and subtlety should read that discussion. It shows how high the view's author stood in wisdom, how firmly grounded he was in knowledge, and how clear his inner vision was—provided the reader has the strength to enter these questions and think them through. Such insight is a gift from God.
VII. The View That Forms of Things Are Present in God's Essence

Avicenna's view, as it appears in many of his books, is this. Sometimes an idea understood by the mind comes from an object in the world. Through sight and careful observation, for example, we form an idea of the heavens, their arrangement, and their shapes. But sometimes the idea does not come from something already perceived. The reverse may happen. A builder first forms an image of a house in his imagination; that image then moves his body until the house is built. In that case, the house's existence in the mind does not come from its existence in the world. Its existence in the world follows its existence in the mind.

In the earlier discussion of mental qualities, we saw that knowledge can be active or receptive. Active knowledge is a cause of the thing known coming to exist in the world. Receptive knowledge comes from the thing already existing. A builder's knowledge of the house he plans is active knowledge, though it is not enough by itself to build the house: he also needs suitable material, tools, a particular place and time, and other conditions.

All things in this world stand in relation to God as a maker's work stands to its maker, or a wise author's book to its author—if that maker's or author's creative power were complete enough that merely conceiving the work brought it into existence. Things proceed from God because He knows them; He does not first find them existing and then know them. God's knowledge of things is like our plans, which we first work out in thought and then bring about. The intelligible form is in some way the cause of the thing's existence. There are, of course, many differences between our thinking and God's knowledge. We are incomplete makers. When we choose to act, we need desire, which arises after we imagine the act. We also need a power to move us, bodily tools such as muscles, tendons, hands, and feet, and external tools such as an axe, chisel, pen, or ink. We need material able to receive the form we intend to give it.

God, by contrast, is complete in existence and in bringing things into being. When He wills something, His command is “Be,” and it is. His command and word, which follow from His eternal essence, are His knowing of things. The existence of things in the world follows their intelligible forms, which are His word. These forms are God's complete words, which never run out. The Qur'an points to this in a striking way: the outer world comes to be through God's word and intellectual command, which accords with His eternal will. We will explain the meaning of God's word and book later, in the Illuminationist way, God willing.

Another argument for saying that God knows things through forms present in His essence begins from this: God knows Himself, and His essence is the cause of things. Complete knowledge of a cause entails knowledge of its effect. So God's knowledge of His own essence would mean that He knows all things eternally. But things did not all exist in reality from eternity. If they also had no intellectual existence in Him, then He would not know them.

Knowledge requires a connection between the knower and what is known. This connection may itself be the relation between them, or it may be a form that establishes the relation. A relation to sheer nonexistence is impossible, because a relation requires both sides to be present in some way. And if things were present in God as parts of His essence, that would make Him composite. So the argument concludes that before things exist in the world, they must exist as intellectual forms in God. These forms must either be separate from Him, which leads to Plato's separate Ideas, or be parts of His essence, which leads to composition. Both are impossible. So, the argument says, the forms must be added to His essence while present in it. This is the view under discussion.

An objection is raised against this reasoning. God's eternal power, too, is related to possible things. His power includes all created things, which come from Him directly or through an intermediary. If the argument required the actual existence of everything God knows, then all created things would have to exist eternally. But created things cannot exist eternally. The proof would therefore fail.

One clever reply says that a relation needs only the assumed existence of its two sides, since the relation itself is only assumed. But the speaker recognizes that this would undermine the whole argument. So he adds that knowledge requires the known thing to be present and revealed to the knower, whereas sheer nonexistence has nothing that can be revealed.

I say: We will return to the original proof. As for the objection based on God's power, we can answer it in this way. Even if power, like knowledge, requires both what acts and what is acted upon, the objection does not succeed. The things God has power over need not exist externally from eternity. Just as it is enough for the things He knows to exist in their forms, it is enough for what He has power over to exist in its forms. These forms are known to Him and also proceed from Him.

The other reply is extremely weak for several reasons. First, it assumes that relations exist only because someone imagines them. But they have a basis in reality whether or not anyone thinks of them. Second, even if relations are not separate things in the world, we derive them from things, and they require the two things being related. Third, that reply arbitrarily distinguishes God's eternal knowledge from His eternal power, although His real attributes are one reality and share one existence. We must not judge His power by our own. In us, power means the capacity and readiness to act; in God, it means making something necessary and bringing it about. His knowledge and His power therefore stand in the same relation to possible things.

Avicenna gives another account in the divine philosophy of The Healing. God knows things, he says, but He cannot know them by receiving knowledge from them. If His essence were shaped by what He knows, then His essence would depend on those things and become composite, which is impossible. Nor can knowledge of things come to Him from outside, since that would introduce a new quality and change Him. The things themselves do not cause His knowledge.

God does not know changing individuals through separate images that multiply and change in His essence. Instead, He knows them as part of a universal order. This does not mean that He knows only general kinds and misses the individual things. The whole chain of causes includes individuals, times, and changes. God knows the causes and how they fit together, and thus knows what must follow from them, including particular events. So He knows individuals through a universal kind of knowledge, not through changing, sensory images.

Anything that receives a new quality from outside must have a receptive capacity, and so must be composite: one aspect is actual, another is only potential. That cannot apply to the Necessary Being, who is simple in every respect.

Nor can God know changing things as changing things, through a separate image for each one. Such images would be changing, perishable, and opposed to one another; God would then be a place where changes and opposites gather. Nor can He know them through sensory or imaginative forms, since these are particular and divided, and need bodily organs. God must know things in another way: intellectually, without change. He knows every thing in a universal way, yet nothing particular escapes Him—not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or earth. This is a remarkable truth, though difficult to grasp.

How does this work? When God knows His own essence and knows that He is the source of everything that exists, He knows the first beings that come from Him and everything that follows from them. Nothing comes into existence unless something makes its existence necessary in some respect; we have already established this. The causes meet and interact until particular events result. God knows those causes, their connections, the outcomes that necessarily follow from them, the times between events, and the patterns that recur. He could not know the causes in full without knowing these consequences. In this way, He knows particular events through the general order of causes.

Avicenna also says: “Do not suppose that if there are many intelligible forms in God, their multiplicity makes them parts of His essence. How could they be parts, when they follow from His essence? His knowledge of His own essence is His essence itself. Through that knowledge He knows what comes after Him. His knowledge of those things follows from His knowledge of Himself. The forms that follow from His essence are present as intellectual objects, not as the images and impressions that arise in our souls. His relation to them is the relation of their source to what proceeds from it, not of a subject that receives them. They follow in an order, one before another in the order of dependence, although there is no earlier or later among them in time. No movement from one act of thought to another occurs there.”

He continues: “The divine world therefore encompasses everything that exists or could exist. God's essence is related to these things as known things, not simply as separate things outside the mind. A further question remains. When they exist as intelligible forms, are they present in the essence of the First as features that necessarily follow from Him? Or do they exist separately from Him and from other beings, as independent forms ordered within the divine domain? Or do they exist within some intellect or soul? On this third view, when that intellect or soul knows the First, the forms become present within it. It is then the subject in which they are known. They are known to that intellect because they are within it, and known to God because they come from Him.”

“God knows from His own essence that He is the source of those intelligible things. Some proceed directly from Him, while others proceed through intermediaries. This must also determine the order of their existence, even if they are all present within one intellect. One comes before another because one causes another, not because of an interval of time.”

“But if the forms present in that other intellect are themselves effects of the First, then they belong to what God knows Himself to produce. We face the difficulty described earlier. Either God's knowing a form brings it into existence, or the form's existence is itself His knowledge of it. If a further act of knowledge were needed, God would first have to know that He knows, and then know that He knows that—and so on without end. If their very existence is His knowledge of them, however, to say ‘They existed because He knew them’ amounts to saying ‘He knew them because He knew them,’ or ‘They existed because they existed.’”

“If these intelligible forms are made into parts of God's essence, multiplicity is introduced into Him. If they are features added to His essence, His essence seems to touch what is possible and thus to acquire a relation that does not belong to what is necessary in itself. If they are independent entities, we arrive at the separate Forms of Plato. And if they exist within another intellect, we encounter the difficulty just described. You must therefore make every effort to resolve this problem while preserving the unity of God's essence.”

“Do not be troubled merely because the divine essence, when considered together with a particular relation, can be described through something possible. Considered as the cause of Zayd's existence, it does not have the same description as it does considered in itself. In itself it is necessary. The divine world is indeed immensely vast. You must also distinguish a thing's giving rise to an image that can be known from its giving rise to a form that is intelligible in the very act of proceeding from it. God knows Himself as the source of every intelligible thing in that very respect, just as He is the source of every existing effect precisely as an existing effect. Think deeply about the principles already laid down and those still to come, so that the truth becomes clear to you.”

That is the end of Avicenna's explanation. Some of it is sound and valuable; some of it is uncertain. Everything in it that supports God's knowledge of things before their external existence, and the presence of their forms in divine knowledge before those things exist, is shared by two different views. One places the forms in God; the other affirms separate Platonic Forms.

Both accounts can accept that God's knowledge of His essence is the source of His knowledge of these forms; that their multiplicity follows from His undivided essence; that they proceed in an order of causes and effects; and that their being known by Him is identical with their proceeding from Him. The forms do not first become known and then exist, or first exist and then become known. They exist as known and are known as existing. Both accounts also accept that God's perfection lies in His essence being the source of these realities, not in His acquiring them as further attributes. What becomes uncertain is the attempt to explain all of this as forms impressed upon a receiving subject. We shall return to that problem.

It is remarkable that those who came after Avicenna and tried to refute this view have not managed to do so. Every objection they have raised comes from too little care in reading his words, a weakness in their own understanding, or too little study of the foundations of philosophy.

Abū al-Barakāt al-Baghdādī argues that if God learned things from them, then something other than God would help complete His essence. But the same reasoning would apply to God as the maker of things: if His making were complete only once the things were made, then those things would complete Him. That is plainly wrong; so, Abū al-Barakāt says, the claim that God learns from things is wrong too.
The reply is that “making” can refer to the relation between maker and made, which comes after both exist.

It can also refer to the source of that relation, which comes first. God's real power to create does not depend on the existence of His effects, because the effects depend on Him. Likewise, God's knowledge should be treated as the source of knowing, not as a relation that comes after the things known.

Suhrawardī, the leader of the Illuminationist school, objects that this view makes God's essence a place for many qualities. Even if God is not changed by them, he says, the account still requires one aspect of God to act and another to receive. It also seems impossible for a being to be the subject of qualities without being described by them.

I agree that a single thing cannot both act and receive an effect when receiving means undergoing a new change. But this does not apply to every case in which a cause produces something and the result depends on that cause. Suppose an effect exists only as a quality of the very cause that necessarily produces it. The act by which it comes from the cause is then the same connection by which it belongs to the cause. The cause produces just this kind of dependent existence. If the effect did not belong to it in that way, the cause would not be producing the effect we are speaking about. So if there is a problem with saying that the first things proceeding from God are qualities, the problem must lie elsewhere. It cannot simply be that producing and receiving are impossible in the same respect.

It is surprising that the critic accepts the necessary features of simple essences, while also saying that those essences themselves are the only causes of these features. Does that not make the same simple essence both the producer of its necessary feature and what the feature belongs to?

His question about how any reasonable person could accept this is aimed at Bahmanyār. In The Attainment, Bahmanyār says that God's essence, though it may be described as the subject of many qualities, is not changed by them and does not acquire new features. His point is that God is not affected by them. We often say that something “has a quality” when the quality changes the subject, as color and taste change a body, or acquired knowledge and power change a soul. But an intellect's own actions and what follows from its activity do not affect it in that way. Nor do the relations it has to things that depend on it. If “having a quality” merely means that something belongs to or follows from a subject, the wording is harmless and does not establish a defect. If it means that the subject becomes something it was not before, no such change follows in this case. The harmless meaning is possible; the harmful meaning is not required.

Suhrawardī raises another objection. Even if God's self-knowledge is not an addition to His essence, one might say that His knowledge of what necessarily follows from Him comes after those consequences. If He knows a consequence because it follows from His nature, then that consequence must first follow from Him before He can know it. In that case, God's knowledge would depend on the consequence. It could not be the cause of the thing's existence, as the philosophers maintain.

I reply that this turns largely on the wording. When philosophers say that God's knowledge of Himself is the cause of His knowledge of what follows from Him, they do not mean that a consequence first exists on its own and is then discovered by God. They mean that God's knowledge of Himself, which is His own essence, gives rise to knowledge of what truly follows from that essence, even where the dependence of the consequence itself is mediated through that knowledge. What follows from a consequence also follows, ultimately, from its first source.

The forms known within God follow from His essence, which is His self-knowledge. Things existing outside Him then follow from His knowledge of those things. They may therefore be called consequences of His consequences. In another respect they are the same consequences, because the form known and the thing existing outside the mind agree in what they are, while differing in their ways of existence—as known in thought and as existing in the world. So there is no contradiction between saying that God's self-knowledge is the cause of His knowledge of what follows from Him and saying that those things come to exist through His knowledge of them.

Suhrawardī then anticipates this reply. He asks: if the forms known by God are present in Him before the separate things that follow from Him, and those things cannot exist without these forms, would God not produce them through His being together with the forms, rather than through His being alone?

I say that those who hold this view do accept that the forms are involved. But this does not close the way to proving the existence of the first intellect. The argument that God is one in every respect, and that His first effect must therefore be one, is not our only proof. First, there are several ways to establish the first intellect and the existence of more than one intellect.

Second, the many aspects that follow from God's being are forms of things existing outside Him. Not every one of these forms can account for just any effect. Each accounts for the thing that corresponds to it, in its proper order.

Third, if proof shows that the forms of things are present in God's knowledge before He brings those things into existence, their existence in the world must agree with how they exist in His knowledge. Their outward conditions and qualities must also agree with their known forms. Otherwise His eternal knowledge would not correspond to what it knows. It would be ignorance, which is impossible.

He then says: “Whether the first form precedes the separate effect or is neither before nor after it, its presence in God's essence would require two aspects in that essence. Nor can the absence of matter be the cause that brings the Necessary Being from an unestablished possibility into actually possessing a form. On that view, His essence would receive the form, while the absence of matter, either alone or together with His essence, would produce it. The absence would then be nobler than His essence: His essence would merely receive, while the absence would determine that the form comes to be and bring it into actuality. But a negative aspect cannot be nobler than the Necessary Being.”

I say: His claim that the first form would require two aspects in God, one for acting and another for receiving, merely repeats his earlier objection. As for his claim about the absence of matter, he has either devised this answer on behalf of his opponents so that he can attack it, or found it in the words of their followers. It rests on a mistake: that whenever something follows from another thing, the first must have been capable of acquiring it, whether or not it follows necessarily and whether or not the first thing brings it about.

That is not so. A source that produces something does not truly lack it and then gain it, either in time or in the order of dependence. Otherwise the source would contain an unfulfilled possibility or capacity. Rather, a thing is more complete in its source than it is when considered in itself, as we have already shown. This is a valuable principle, understood by only a few.

He then objects that the first form, together with the First, would produce two different effects: the first effect itself and another form. I reply, first, that his objection applies equally to the first intellect, which is said to cause both the second intellect and the outermost sphere. More fundamentally, the first form is not one in the same absolute way as the Necessary Being. Everything other than God includes both perfection and limitation, and each aspect has its own effects: what is nobler gives rise to what is nobler, and what is lower gives rise to what is lower.

I say: you already know that, on this account, the forms do not add any perfection to His essence. His knowledge that truly belongs among His perfections is identical with His essence. These forms proceed from Him just as other existing things proceed from Him. They come from His essence, and their existence and their necessity depend on Him. In relation to Him they are necessary and actual, not merely possible or waiting to become actual.

There is no contradiction in saying that something is possible when considered in relation to its own nature, yet necessary when considered in relation to its cause. The existence of each form is at once its existence in itself and its existence as something known to the Necessary Being. That does not make its existence merely possible in relation to Him. To call an existence possible means that it has a nature distinct from its existence and, when measured against that nature alone, could either exist or not exist. It does not mean that the existence is in a state of possibility in itself, in reality, or in relation to the cause from which it cannot be separated.

In short, the presence of these forms does not remove any weakness or lack in the Necessary Being; nor does their absence mean that He has lost something. His perfection and glory consist in His being such that the forms proceed from Him. They do not consist in His acquiring those forms, or even in the forms' existence considered on its own. His perfection belongs to His essence, not to something else.
Avicenna makes this point repeatedly. In his Annotations he writes:

Suppose the First understands Himself as the source of those things, and suppose they then exist in Him. Does their existence in Him affect His understanding of them, or does it not? If it does, their existence is the cause of His understanding them. Yet their existence is itself caused by His understanding them. We would then be saying that He understands them because He understands them, or that they come from Him because they come from Him.

If the existence of those things as objects of thought caused the First to understand them, while His understanding caused their existence, we would simply be saying that they came from Him because they came from Him. If His understanding caused their existence, but their existence then caused His understanding, we would be saying that He understood them because He understood them. Both accounts are impossible. The truth is that their being understood by Him is itself their existence as proceeding from Him.

The First does not learn about existing things from their existence, for He gives them existence. He knows them as proceeding from Him. His knowledge of Himself is knowledge of them because they follow necessarily from Him. He brings them into existence as things already known, not as things that first exist and then become fit to be known.

Someone may say that He knows things before they exist. But this would seem to mean either that He knows them while they do not exist, or that He knows them only when they exist, so that He learns of them from their existence. That way of putting it is mistaken. His knowledge of them is their very existence, and their being objects of His knowledge is their being existent. He does not know things by first receiving them within Himself, as we know things when they become present to us. Their being present to Him is His knowledge of them, and His knowledge is simple.

He then says, in effect: “To claim that forms exist in the Necessary Being is a false claim and a poor belief. It would mean that something higher than His essence supplies Him with the forms, which is impossible. And if its defenders admit that one and the same thing, in the same respect, can both receive and act, they destroy many of their own important principles and accept numerous contradictions.” That is the end of his statement.

My reply is this. We know that the Necessary Being is the source of everything and the source of the necessity through which things exist. When something comes from Him through an intermediate cause, that cause too comes from Him. Every power to act therefore has its source in Him, and every excellence is a gift flowing from His excellence. Nothing can add anything to Him. How could the things He gives existence to increase a perfection that was not already His through His own essence?

We also know that the source of a feature and the subject to which it belongs need not always be distinct. Consider the features that follow necessarily from a thing's essence. In this discussion, to call something a receiver does not mean that it undergoes a change or is affected from outside. Nothing in this claim, properly understood, overturns a philosophical principle.

Of course, if someone claimed without qualification that one thing could act and receive an action in precisely the same respect, important rules would be undermined. The soul, for example, has been said to need different powers for receiving impressions and preserving them: common sensation and imagination, or estimation and memory. The power that senses receives and is affected; the power that preserves an impression acts. Natural philosophers likewise distinguish wetness from dryness, the capacity for movement from the power that moves something, and sensation from movement.

The same mistake would affect the account of bodies as composed of matter and form. A body, as a body, already has the definite reality of an extended substance, but it is also capable of receiving other states. Its form explains what it already is; its matter explains its capacity to become something else.

But the proof that God's attributes are identical with His essence does not rest solely on saying that, if they were added to Him, one and the same being would have to act and receive. We gave a different argument in the discussion of the divine attributes. God, after all, has many ordered relations to created things, and these do not force us to posit separate sides in Him, one acting and one receiving.

In short, despite the long history of objections, I do not see that the critics have yet shown the claim that intelligible forms exist in the Necessary Being to be a corrupt belief or an incoherent position. There remains the argument that I shall present, with the help of God, the Mighty and Wise.

Another determined opponent of these forms was Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, in his commentary on Avicenna's Pointers and Reminders. This is surprising, since at the start of his sections on nature and theology he had promised not to disagree with Avicenna's beliefs. I wish he had kept that promise here too. It would have served him better until God opened his heart to what is right.
Al-Tusi set out what he regarded as the problems with saying that forms exist within God's essence. He wrote:

“To say that the necessary consequences of the First exist within His essence is to say that one and the same being both acts and receives. It is to say that the First has attributes that are neither relations nor negations. It makes Him a subject in which His many possible effects exist—far exalted is He above that. It also means that the first effect is not separate from His essence, and that He brings nothing distinct from Himself into existence except through things that reside within Him.

“Such claims conflict with what appears to be the teaching of the philosophers. Earlier thinkers denied knowledge to God. Plato held that intelligible forms exist independently; the followers of Aristotle held that the knower and the known become one; and the Mu'tazilites held that things which do not exist nevertheless have an established reality. They took on these impossible positions in order to avoid the implications just listed.”

I say that the first objection—that God would both act and receive—works only if receiving means undergoing a new change, or if what is received adds a perfection God did not already have. If 'receiving' merely means that something necessarily follows from His essence, no contradiction has been shown. Anyone who means something more must prove it.

Avicenna says in his Annotations: “The One who must exist cannot receive something that makes Him what He is, since receiving in this sense involves a capacity not yet fulfilled. Nor can we simply say that qualities arise in Him from His own essence and make Him a receiver as well as an agent. There is, however, a different case: qualities that necessarily follow from His essence. They are present in Him because they proceed from Him; He does not acquire them from elsewhere. Consider the difference between saying a body is white because whiteness comes to it from outside, and saying, if this were possible for a body, that it is white because whiteness follows from its own nature. On this understanding, the First and what necessarily follows from Him do not introduce several things into His essence. There is no separate receiver and agent. In the very respect in which He is called a receiver, He is the agent. The same holds for every simple reality: what follows from it and is present in it does not divide it. In a thing that has parts, by contrast, what something proceeds from can differ from the part in which it is present.”

Avicenna adds that this applies to everything that necessarily follows from a simple reality. He writes: “There is no readiness in simple things. Readiness means that something can come to be in a thing through another cause after it was absent, and the readiness must exist before that reception. The human soul cannot both produce intellectual forms and receive them after lacking them, because that would require an earlier capacity. But something whose nature is always accompanied by what it understands does not need an unrealized capacity. What receives an intellectual form cannot, in the same respect, be the source that produces it, when neither activity was there before. Such a change presupposes a capacity.”
